newsitem.title: USA: Energy Dept seeks NRC as "external" regulator.
newsitem.headline: Energy Dept seeks NRC as "external" regulator.

text.p: The Energy Department said on Friday it would ask Congress to transfer oversight of the safety of its various nuclear sites, including those contaminated during the arms race, from the department to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).

"We feel external regulation is the best way to instill public confidence" in the department's activities that include cleanup of contaminated former nuclear weapons production and testing sites, treatment of nuclear waste, maintaining the weapons stockpile and research, Undersecretary Thomas Grumbly said at a briefing.

"Independent safety regulation will provide a safer and healthier environment for our workers throughout the complex and the public around our sites," Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said in a statement.

The department plans to submit legislation to phase in the transfer of oversight responsiblities over 10 years to the NRC, gradually shifting responsibilities from the department itself and from an independent board that oversees safety of some of the department's defense-related activities.

"I think this is a step in the right direction, but the NRC has to put some elements of its own house in order before it regulates the DOE," Arjun Makhijani, president of the Institute for Energy and Environmental Research, said.
Makhijani also said he was concerned that current rules of the NRC could limit the public's access to information and to the courts.
Lawsuits by people living near contaminated sites and environmental groups have been a key to spurring the government's efforts to clean up the radioactive legacy of the nuclear arms race.

The NRC has not taken a firm position on whether it wants to become the Energy Department's overseer, although NRC Chairwoman Shirley Jackson has said her agency would be the appropriate body for that.
"It's going to depend on resources by Congress and a time schedule to develop an appropriate regulatory program," NRC spokesman Joe Gilliland said.

The Energy Department estimated that the cost of external regulation would be about $135 million annually. But it said overall safety and health costs for the department's nuclear facilities still should drop significantly as a number of sites are slated to be closed.
